title: Accessibility isn't an audit at the end of the project. It's product quality.
description: Accessibility handled only at the end becomes a list of fixes. Bring it into the brief, the design system and testing with people.

related.title: Clint Scale
related.body: In practice: a design system with documented tokens, states and components to keep things consistent at scale.

blocks.text: Accessibility usually shows up late in the process: after the layout is done, when someone checks contrast, adds an attribute or tries to navigate with a keyboard.
That path turns accessibility into a list of fixes and raises the chance of finding structural problems when there's little time left to change the interface.
The more useful approach is to treat accessibility as part of product quality, from defining the problem to validating the solution.
Start with the flow, not just the component
A button can have adequate contrast and still be hard to use if keyboard focus doesn't show, if the label doesn't explain the action or if the loading state isn't announced to assistive technologies.
Evaluating isolated components isn't enough. Look at the whole flow: how the person gets to the task, understands the content, interacts, receives feedback, fixes errors and completes the action.
Accessibility lives in the combination of content, behavior, semantic structure, focus, states and the technology used.
Include accessibility in the brief
Before designing, write down questions like:

items: Can the flow be completed without a mouse?
Does the focus order follow the reading order?
Does the error explain how to fix the problem?
Is the information understandable without relying only on color?
Does the content stay readable when zoomed?
Do components have focus, error, success and disabled states?
Is the content compatible with screen readers?

blocks.text: Not every question will be equally relevant in every project, but they help keep accessibility from being treated as a visual tweak at the end.
Contrast matters, but it isn't everything
Contrast, visible focus, size and spacing affect readability. But conformance depends on specific criteria and contexts, like text size, component type and content.
Use contrast tools as support, not as the only validation. Check hierarchy, zoom, focus, keyboard navigation, semantics, status messages and behavior across different devices.
Don't claim an interface is “100% accessible” because it passed a plugin or an automated audit. Automated tools catch some problems, but they don't replace manual testing and evaluation with people.
A design system can prevent problems at scale
If every team implements focus, errors, modals, fields and success messages in its own way, consistency gets hard to maintain.
A design system can include:

items: Color tokens validated for specific uses
Components with documented semantics and behavior
Examples of correct and incorrect use

blocks.text: Documenting isn't enough. It's important to test components in real code and review how they behave in complete flows.
Test with different people and technologies
A practical evaluation can combine keyboard navigation, screen readers, zoom, contrast checks, automated audits and task testing with people who have different access needs.

These approaches find different kinds of problems. An automated audit can flag a missing accessible name, but it can't tell on its own whether the text helps the person complete the task. A usability test can reveal confusion in the flow that never shows up on a technical checklist.
Plan time to fix and retest. Finding a problem without validating the fix leaves the work unfinished.
Measure accessibility as part of quality

There's no single metric that captures all of accessibility. Pick indicators tied to the product's risks and tasks, like completing a task with a keyboard, form errors, task success with a screen reader or critical barriers identified and fixed.

Use these measures carefully: the result of a small session doesn't automatically represent all people with disabilities. Combine indicators, audits and feedback, and record which scenarios were evaluated.
Accessibility isn't just compliance. It's making sure more people can understand, navigate and use the product on their own.
